synthesis.hadamard-deposit-premise.formal:
\emph{Premise (HD), the deposit is Hadamard.} Units $\hbar = c = 1$. Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be the descended gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), on the region after the descent, and suppose its derived metric is smooth and globally hyperbolic there. A \emph{Cauchy collar of the descent} is an open neighbourhood $N$, in that region and adjacent to the descent, of a Cauchy surface $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ of it. The deposited state $\omega_{d}$ is the state in which the descent leaves the free fields of the descended phase: for the fermion modes a gauge-invariant quasi-free state, the vacuum plus quanta (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.quasi-free-deposit-is-vacuum-plus-shot-noise}), and for each free scalar field of the descended phase the quasi-free state the descent sets (as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-descent-as-vacuum}). The premise: \emph{there is a Cauchy collar $N$ of the descent on which $\omega_{d}$ is Hadamard}, that is, for the free Dirac field of each mass $\mathrm{WF}'(\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}) = C^{(\pm)}$ on $N \times N$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(b)), and for each free scalar field $\mathrm{WF}'(\Lambda) = C^{+}$ on $N \times N$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(a)).

\emph{Equivalent form, and the free data.} Let an \emph{admissible reference vacuum} on $N$ be, for a massless conformally covariant field, the conformal vacuum where the field is Weyl-flat (Hadamard there: Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weyl-flat-fields-need-no-scaling-limit-premise-and-robertson-walker-generators-see-the-schwarzian}(i) for the Dirac field), and, for a massive Dirac field on a Robertson-Walker collar, a homogeneous state adiabatic of infinite order with $M = ma$ smooth (Hadamard: Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-propagates-and-adiabatic-states-are-hadamard}(c)). Since Hadamard two-point functions differ by smooth kernels (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}), (HD) says that the two-point functions of $\omega_{d}$ differ from those of an admissible reference vacuum by smooth kernels on $N \times N$. The occupation (Bogoliubov) profile of $\omega_{d}$ over that reference is free data: (HD) fixes only its ultraviolet tail.

\emph{What it is for.} (1) \emph{Hadamard states on every later field.} By the propagation of the Hadamard form (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-propagation-of-hadamard-form} for the scalar field, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-propagates-and-adiabatic-states-are-hadamard}(b) for the Dirac field), $\omega_{d}$ is Hadamard on the whole domain of dependence of $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$: every later field it determines, regions of nonzero Weyl curvature and holes formed by collapse included, up to any Cauchy horizon, where the domain of dependence ends (and where, on the Reissner-Nordstr\"om-de Sitter field, the stress tensor of every Hadamard scalar state generically diverges, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-hadamard-stress-tensor-diverges-at-the-reissner-nordstrom-de-sitter-cauchy-horizon}). (2) \emph{The local form of (N$_{+}$) at every horizon.} On Weyl-flat regions every quasi-free Hadamard state of the massless Dirac field has the local form of (N$_{+}$) at every point of every local Rindler horizon, at the leading order at which those horizons are defined, with no further premise (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weyl-flat-fields-need-no-scaling-limit-premise-and-robertson-walker-generators-see-the-schwarzian}(ii)); at points of nonzero Weyl curvature, and for massive fields, it follows by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.hadamard-scaling-limit-premise}, (HS) (formerly a premise), with Theorem \claimref{synthesis.bulk-hadamard-states-restrict-to-the-generator-condition-on-flat-null-planes}. So the open premise that the series' states are Hadamard on horizon generators is supplied, for the local form of (N$_{+}$), by (HD), the propagation Facts and (HS). (3) \emph{The collapse result's state.} For a hole formed by collapse inside that domain, the propagated deposit is Hadamard at the horizon, and its short-distance form on the ingoing sheet, the condition (N$_{+}^{\mathrm{coll}}$) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.collapsing-hole-flux-from-ground-state-on-the-ingoing-sheet}(v), follows given (HS) at the horizon point (argued: that result works with the s-wave reduction of its modes). (4) \emph{The renormalised stress tensor.} On the same domain the expected stress tensor of the Dirac part of $\omega_{d}$ is defined and covariantly conserved (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-renormalised-stress-tensor-of-hadamard-dirac-states}); for the scalar fields the corresponding Hadamard point splitting is standard and not imported.

\emph{What it does not give.} (1) \emph{Which state.} The occupation profile over an admissible reference vacuum stays free. For the massless Dirac field on a Robertson-Walker collar, a homogeneous deposit diagonal over the conformal vacuum satisfies (HD) exactly when every moment of its occupation profile is finite, and the thermal deposit does (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.deposit-over-the-conformal-vacuum-is-hadamard-exactly-when-every-occupation-moment-is-finite}); the number and energy spread of the quanta do not decide it. For the massive Dirac field (HD) excludes the instantaneous vacuum at an instant where $ma' \neq 0$, every deposit diagonal over it, and every state carried through a descent across which $M = ma$ is not smooth (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.massive-dirac-instantaneous-vacuum-and-non-smooth-descents-are-not-hadamard}). Neither the wall's smoothness nor the descent's conditional expectation selects a state (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.radical-normal-tame-wall-is-a-regular-initial-surface-whose-smoothness-selects-no-state}), and no locally covariant choice of state exists. (2) \emph{The ground-state clause of (N$_{+}$).} Every Hadamard state passes the local form, thermal ones included; on a Robertson-Walker field the conformal vacuum is the ground state of the physical affine translations on every null generator only on de Sitter and flat fields (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weyl-flat-fields-need-no-scaling-limit-premise-and-robertson-walker-generators-see-the-schwarzian}(iii)). (3) \emph{The spectrum, the deposit's infrared datum.} Relative to a homogeneous Hadamard reference, (HD) leaves the amplitude and index of the spectrum free on every bounded band, allows a power-law ratio for the conformally coupled field on no band unbounded toward short scales, and, by the infrared divergence (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-ford-parker-infrared-divergence}), a red law on no band reaching $k = 0$ for slice fields of nonzero mean; a red band needs ends $k_{\mathrm{IR}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{UV}}$ that (HD) does not fix (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.hadamard-condition-leaves-the-deposit-spectrum-free-on-bounded-bands}). (4) Anything beyond the domain of dependence of the collar. ((HS) at points of nonzero Weyl curvature or for massive fields, listed here before, is now Theorem \claimref{synthesis.hadamard-scaling-limit-premise}.)

\emph{Relation to the descent's normal form.} (HD) needs only a Cauchy collar on the descended side; the normal form of the descent is not part of it. Under the radiation-type descent, a stated hypothesis of the results that need it and not a postulate, the descent is conformally a radical-normal tame wall, the descended side is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy slices from any collar (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.radical-normal-tame-wall-is-a-regular-initial-surface-whose-smoothness-selects-no-state}(i), (iv)), the collar is Weyl-flat, the conformal vacuum is an admissible reference for the conformally covariant fields, and $M = ma$ is smooth at the origin, so the jump law of the massive result does not fire there. On the Kasner branch, Premises \claimref{synthesis.pre-descent-contracting-kasner-stage-premise} (P1) and \claimref{synthesis.pre-descent-state-carried-into-descended-phase-premise} (P2), the four-dimensional Kasner approach is Weyl-curved except at the Milne and isotropic points (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.kasner-field-is-weyl-flat-only-at-the-milne-and-isotropic-points}), the wall is a curvature singularity and no conformal vacuum is available as reference; there (HD) asserts that the state carried by (P2) into the descended phase is Hadamard on a collar after the descent.

\emph{Refutation condition.} The premise is false if either of the following is established: (a) a derivation from the series' premises that the deposited state fails the Hadamard condition on every Cauchy collar of the descent, for example that the descent deposits, for a massive Dirac field, the instantaneous vacuum where $ma' \neq 0$ or a state diagonal over it, or the tracial state (occupation one half at every momentum), or an occupation profile with an infinite moment over the conformal vacuum, or that $M = ma$ is not smooth across the descent (a kink or jump in the scale factor or its derivatives); (b) an observation of a relic free field of the descended phase whose occupation numbers over the vacuum fall off at large momentum no faster than a power, at arbitrarily large momentum, which no Hadamard state has.

\emph{Note (the spin-product selection, 2 November 2026).} One candidate for deriving (HD), selecting the deposit by the Dirac field's own spin product (the Fewster-Lang weighted spin-product state on a collar, the finite-time form of the fermionic projector state; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-fewster-lang-spin-product-states-of-the-dirac-field}), is ruled out for massless fields: the spin product is odd under chirality, so the selected state is Hadamard on no open set of any collar on which its operator is injective, torsion included, with occupation one half over the conformal vacuum on Robertson-Walker collars for every weight; for massive fields it is Hadamard only with a smooth time weight (\claimref{synthesis.spin-product-state-of-the-massless-dirac-field-is-odd-under-chirality-and-never-hadamard}). The premise is unchanged.
synthesis.hadamard-deposit-premise.technical:
The series' field theory on a gravitational field needs a state, and the store's chain from the descent to the later fields lacked one datum: that the state the descent deposits is of the regular, Hadamard kind. This premise supplies it, as an assumption: there is a thin collar after the descent, a neighbourhood of a Cauchy surface, on which the deposited state of the Dirac field and of the scalar fields is Hadamard. Equivalently, its two-point functions differ by smooth kernels from those of an admissible reference vacuum: the conformal vacuum for massless conformally covariant fields where the field is Weyl-flat, and an adiabatic state of infinite order, with the mass term $ma$ smooth, for massive Dirac fields. The occupation profile above that reference is left free; the premise fixes only its high-momentum tail.

With the imported propagation of the Hadamard form, for the scalar and the Dirac field, the deposited state is then Hadamard on every later field in the collar's domain of dependence, regions of nonzero Weyl curvature and collapsing holes included, up to any Cauchy horizon. On Weyl-flat regions the local form of (N$_{+}$) follows for the massless Dirac field with no further premise; elsewhere it follows by the scaling-limit theorem (HS). The collapse result's short-distance condition follows, argued, given (HS) at the horizon point, and the renormalised stress tensor of the Dirac field is defined and conserved.

It does not say which state is deposited (for the massless Dirac field any diagonal profile with all moments finite, the thermal one included; for massive fields not the instantaneous vacuum and not a descent with a kink); it does not give the ground-state clause of (N$_{+}$); and it does not give the spectrum, which stays the deposit's infrared datum: free on bounded bands, with ends at both large and small scales that it does not fix. The descent's normal form is separate: under the radiation-type reading, a stated hypothesis, the collar is Weyl-flat and the conformal vacuum is available; under the Kasner branch the state carried across the wall must itself be Hadamard after it. It would be refuted by a derivation that the descent deposits a non-Hadamard state, such as the instantaneous vacuum of a massive field, or through a non-smooth descent, or by a relic field whose occupations fall off only as a power at arbitrarily high momentum.

(Note, 2 November 2026: selecting the deposit by the Dirac field's own spin product is ruled out for massless fields, where the selected state is never Hadamard, so that candidate does not derive this premise, \claimref{synthesis.spin-product-state-of-the-massless-dirac-field-is-odd-under-chirality-and-never-hadamard}.)
synthesis.hadamard-deposit-premise.lay: Quantum fields in a gravitational field make sense only in well-behaved states, called Hadamard states, which look like empty space at very short distances. The series' account of the universe's earliest moment, the descent, leaves its fields in some state, but nothing in the series yet shows that state is well behaved. This premise assumes it: just after the descent the state is of the well-behaved kind. Since good behaviour, once present, is kept by the equations of motion, every later situation, including black holes formed by collapse, then has well-behaved states, which is what the series' horizon results and the energy of quantum fields need. The premise does not say which well-behaved state it is, how many particles of each energy were left behind, or what pattern of primordial ripples they carry; those remain open inputs.

synthesis.imported-adler-bell-jackiw-axi.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$, signature $(+,-,-,-)$, $\alpha = e^{2}/(4\pi)$. For a Dirac fermion of mass $m$ and charge $e$ coupled to the electromagnetic field $F$, with the axial current $j^{5}_{\mu} = \bar\psi\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}\psi$ and the pseudoscalar density $j^{5} = \bar\psi\gamma_{5}\psi$ (index reading of the sources), the one-loop triangle graph with one axial and two vector vertices cannot be made to conserve the vector current and to satisfy the naive axial Ward identity at once; keeping the vector current conserved,
\[
\partial^{\mu}j^{5}_{\mu} = 2im\,j^{5} + \frac{\alpha}{4\pi}\,\epsilon_{\xi\sigma\tau\rho}F^{\xi\sigma}F^{\tau\rho}
\]
\cite{Adler1969} (in the form of \cite{Adler2004}, eq. (1), with bare $m$ and $\alpha$). The anomalous term is proportional to $E\cdot B$, the pseudoscalar part of the square of the field-strength bivector. In the $\sigma$-model the same term removes the conflict between partial conservation of the axial current and the observed rate of $\pi^{0} \to \gamma\gamma$ \cite{BellJackiw1969}.
synthesis.imported-adler-bell-jackiw-axi.technical: The axial anomaly is the failure of the classical conservation law of the axial current of a massless fermion in the quantum theory. Adler computed the triangle graph with one axial and two vector vertices in spinor electrodynamics and showed that, when the vector current is kept conserved (as gauge invariance requires), the divergence of the axial current acquires a term proportional to the electromagnetic field contracted with its dual, $E\cdot B$, with coefficient $\alpha/(4\pi)$ in the normalisation $\epsilon FF$. Bell and Jackiw found the same term in the $\sigma$-model and showed that it accounts for the decay of the neutral pion into two photons, which the naive current algebra forbids.
synthesis.imported-adler-bell-jackiw-axi.lay: Some symmetries of the classical equations of particle physics do not survive in the quantum theory. The best known case concerns the difference between left-handed and right-handed particles: in 1969 Adler, and Bell and Jackiw, found that quantum effects of light break this balance by an amount set by the electric and magnetic fields together, and that this explains why a neutral pion decays into two photons. The series takes this result from the literature.

J. S. Bell and R. Jackiw, A PCAC puzzle: pi0 -> gamma gamma in the sigma-model, Nuovo Cimento A 60 (1969), 47--61.
S. L. Adler, Anomalies to all orders, in: 50 Years of Yang-Mills Theory, ed. G. 't Hooft, World Scientific (2005); arXiv:hep-th/0405040.

synthesis.imported-bochner-theorem-momen.technical: Three classical lemmas of analysis. Bochner's theorem says that the functions of one real variable that are continuous and positive definite are exactly the Fourier transforms of finite positive measures. The moment lemma of probability theory says that smoothness of such a transform at the origin controls the measure's tail: a derivative of even order $2k$ at the origin forces the moment of order $2k$ to be finite. Whitney's theorem says that a smooth even function of one variable is a smooth function of the square of that variable, and so a smooth odd one is the variable times such a function.
synthesis.imported-bochner-theorem-momen.lay: These are three standard results of mathematical analysis. One says which functions arise as averages of waves with positive weights; another says that if such an average is smooth at its centre, the weights must fall off fast at high frequencies; the third says that a smooth function that is symmetric about zero can be written as a smooth function of the square of its argument. They are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-brst-kugo-ojima-stroc.technical: These are the standard foundations of the covariant quantisation of gauge fields. Becchi, Rouet and Stora, and independently Tyutin, found that the gauge-fixed action with ghosts keeps a nilpotent fermionic symmetry, now called BRST, whose charge defines the physical states as a cohomology. Kugo and Ojima showed that when this charge is self-adjoint for an indefinite inner product, the unphysical modes (timelike and longitudinal photons, ghosts and antighosts) pair into quartets of zero norm, so the physical states have positive norm and the physical scattering is unitary. Strocchi proved that the indefinite metric cannot be avoided: on a positive-metric space a local covariant vector potential satisfying Maxwell's equations has trivial field strength. Gribov showed that the usual non-abelian gauge conditions do not pick a unique representative of each gauge orbit beyond small fields, so the ghost construction is a perturbative tool.
synthesis.imported-brst-kugo-ojima-stroc.lay: Force fields such as light and the gluons carry a redundancy: many mathematical descriptions give the same physics. Removing it while keeping the equal treatment of space and time is done with fictitious ghost particles and a bookkeeping symmetry found in the 1970s. That bookkeeping works only if some unphysical states are allowed negative or zero length, which then cancel in groups of four; a theorem of Strocchi shows there is no way around this, and Gribov showed that for the gluons the usual way of removing the redundancy fails for very strong fields. The series takes these results from the literature.

synthesis.imported-conformal-covariance-.technical: Two classical facts of conformal geometry. First, a four-dimensional gravitational field whose Weyl curvature vanishes is, near each point, a rescaling of the flat field by a smooth positive factor (Weyl and Schouten; in four or more dimensions the Weyl tensor is the complete local obstruction to conformal flatness). Second, the massless fields of the standard model are conformally covariant in four dimensions: under a rescaling of the metric by $\varphi^{2}$ a solution of the massless Dirac equation is carried to a solution by the factor $\varphi^{-3/2}$, a conformally coupled massless scalar by $\varphi^{-1}$, and the Maxwell and Yang-Mills equations are unchanged. The maps preserve the conserved current or symplectic form, so the quantum field algebras are identified. Together they let the conformal vacuum of a Weyl-flat field be the flat vacuum, rescaled.
synthesis.imported-conformal-covariance-.lay: Some gravitational fields are, up to a change of scale from place to place, the same as empty flat space: exactly those in which gravity stretches but does not distort shapes. Massless particles, such as light and massless electrons, cannot tell a change of scale apart, so on such fields their physics is that of flat space, rescaled. These are classical results, taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-dimensional-regularis.formal:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Dimensional regularisation.)} Loop integrals are continued in the spacetime dimension $D$ and their divergences appear as poles at $D = 4$; the continuation preserves Lorentz invariance and, for vector-like gauge theories, gauge invariance \cite{tHooftVeltman1972}.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The BMHV $\gamma_{5}$.)} In the scheme of 't Hooft and Veltman and of Breitenlohner and Maison the $D$-dimensional metric splits as $g = \bar g + \hat g$ into a four-dimensional and a $(D-4)$-dimensional (evanescent) part, the Dirac matrices correspondingly as $\gamma^{\mu} = \bar\gamma^{\mu} + \hat\gamma^{\mu}$ with $\{\bar\gamma^{\mu}, \hat\gamma^{\nu}\} = 0$, and $\gamma_{5}$, the four-dimensional product, satisfies $\{\gamma_{5}, \bar\gamma^{\mu}\} = 0$ and $[\gamma_{5}, \hat\gamma^{\mu}] = 0$. In chiral gauge theories this breaks BRST invariance; the singular and evanescent counterterms are not gauge invariant, and finite counterterms restore the symmetry; at one loop the renormalisation group equations are unchanged \cite{BreitenlohnerMaison1977, BeluscaMaito2020}.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The obstruction.)} No $\gamma_{5}$ anticommuting with every $\gamma^{\mu}$ in $D \neq 4$ is compatible with a cyclic trace and $\mathrm{Tr}(\gamma_{5}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\nu}\gamma^{\rho}\gamma^{\sigma}) \neq 0$ \cite{BreitenlohnerMaison1977}.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The $d$-dimensional integral rules.)} On the Euclidean section, with measure $d^{d}\ell/\pi^{d/2}$, $d = 4 - 2\epsilon$: integrals are invariant under shifts of the loop momentum, $\int d^{d}\ell\,f(\ell + p) = \int d^{d}\ell\,f(\ell)$ \cite{Weinzierl2010}; scale-free integrals vanish, $\int d^{d}\ell\,Q(\ell)^{-a} = 0$, and so do integrals of total derivatives, which gives the integration-by-parts identities, among them the triangle rule \cite{ChetyrkinTkachov1981, Grozin2003, KotikovTeber2018}; the radial integral is $\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{\pi^{d/2}}\,\frac{Q(\ell)^{r}}{(Q(\ell) + \Delta)^{N}} = \frac{\Gamma(r + d/2)\,\Gamma(N - r - d/2)}{\Gamma(d/2)\,\Gamma(N)}\,\Delta^{d/2 + r - N}$, and under the integral $\ell^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\ell^{\alpha_{2r}} \to Q(\ell)^{r}\{\delta^{r}\}/(d(d+2)\cdots(d + 2r - 2))$, $\{\delta^{r}\}$ the sum over the pairings of the indices (symmetric integration); the Minkowski forms follow by the Wick rotation. The massless one-loop bubble is
\[
\int\frac{d^{d}k}{\pi^{d/2}}\,\frac{1}{Q(k)^{a_{1}}\,Q(k - q)^{a_{2}}} = G(a_{1}, a_{2})\,Q(q)^{d/2 - a_{1} - a_{2}}, \qquad G(a_{1}, a_{2}) = \frac{\Gamma(a_{1} + a_{2} - d/2)\,\Gamma(d/2 - a_{1})\,\Gamma(d/2 - a_{2})}{\Gamma(a_{1})\,\Gamma(a_{2})\,\Gamma(d - a_{1} - a_{2})}
\]
\cite{Grozin2003, KotikovTeber2018}, and the two-loop massless self-energy integral with five lines of unit index, $\int\int\frac{d^{d}k\,d^{d}l}{\pi^{d}}\,\frac{1}{Q(k)Q(k - q)Q(l)Q(l - q)Q(k - l)}$, equals $6\zeta_{3}/Q(q) + O(\epsilon)$ \cite{ChetyrkinTkachov1981, KotikovTeber2018}.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Two loops in the abelian chiral theory.)} For an abelian gauge theory with right-handed fermions of charges $\mathcal{Y}_{R}$ and $\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathcal{Y}_{R}^{3} = 0$, the BMHV scheme is consistent at two loops: the finite symmetry-restoring counterterms through two loops have the same form as at one loop, restoring the Ward identities, the one-loop ones being $\frac{\hbar}{16\pi^{2}}\int\bigl[-\frac{e^{2}}{6}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{Y}_{R}^{2})\,\bar A\cdot\bar\partial^{2}\bar A + \frac{e^{4}}{12}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{Y}_{R}^{4})\,(\bar A^{2})^{2} + (\text{a fermion term proportional to } 5 + \xi)\bigr]$; ultraviolet-divergent evanescent counterterms are needed in addition \cite{BeluscaMaito2021}.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.imported-dimensional-regularis.technical:
Dimensional regularisation continues loop integrals to a non-integer number of dimensions, so divergences become poles at four dimensions; it keeps Lorentz and vector-like gauge invariance. The chirality matrix $\gamma_{5}$ is intrinsically four-dimensional, and no continuation keeps it anticommuting with every Dirac matrix while traces stay cyclic and the four-dimensional epsilon trace survives. The standard consistent choice, due to 't Hooft and Veltman and to Breitenlohner and Maison, splits the Dirac matrices into a four-dimensional part, with which $\gamma_{5}$ anticommutes, and an evanescent part, with which it commutes. In chiral gauge theories this breaks the BRST symmetry, and finite counterterms are needed to restore it; for an abelian theory with right-handed fermions their form at two loops is the same as at one loop (Belusca-Maito and collaborators, 2021).

The rules that make dimensionally continued integrals computable are also standard. Integrals do not change when the loop momentum is shifted, integrals with no scale and integrals of total derivatives vanish, and the last gives the integration-by-parts identities of Chetyrkin and Tkachov, which reduce massless multi-loop integrals to a few masters. The one-loop radial integral and the massless bubble are ratios of Gamma functions; under the integral, products of loop momenta are replaced by symmetric combinations of the metric over $d(d+2)\cdots$; and the two-loop self-energy integral with five unit lines is $6\zeta_{3}$ at four dimensions.
synthesis.imported-dimensional-regularis.lay: One standard way of taming the infinities of quantum corrections pretends that spacetime has a slightly non-integer number of dimensions. The quantity that distinguishes left-handed from right-handed particles exists only in four dimensions, so the method has to give up one of its properties; the standard choice keeps it consistent at the cost of extra corrections in theories, like the weak force, that treat left and right differently. The method comes with a small set of rules for doing the resulting integrals, which reduce complicated calculations to a few standard ones.

synthesis.imported-dimock-dirac-car-alge.technical: Before one can ask for a quantum state of the Dirac field in a gravitational field, the field itself, as an algebra of operators, has to exist. Dimock showed that on every spacetime with a well-posed initial-value problem (globally hyperbolic) the free Dirac field exists, with anticommutators that vanish at spacelike separation, and that its algebras of local observables satisfy the standard axioms of algebraic quantum field theory in a form adapted to curved backgrounds. In the store's language: on every gravitational field with a globally hyperbolic derived metric the Dirac CAR algebra exists; what is not fixed is a state, which is a separate datum. The same construction shows that the anticommutator of two smeared fields is the conserved inner product (the flux of the current through any instant) of the classical solutions they define, and that the causal propagator rebuilds every solution from its values at one instant.
synthesis.imported-dimock-dirac-car-alge.lay: The rules of quantum field theory for electrons and similar particles can be set up in any reasonable gravitational field: the field's operators exist and respect causality. Dimock proved this in 1982. What the construction does not provide is a choice of the quantum state, the analogue of empty space, which has to be supplied separately. This is taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-p.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is smooth and globally hyperbolic, read on several charts where its global structure needs them, and let $\psi$ be the free Dirac field of mass $m \ge 0$ on it, quantised by the canonical anticommutation relations, with the two two-point functions $\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}$ of a quasi-free state $\omega$ and the sets $C^{(\pm)}$ of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(b).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Equivalence; Sahlmann and Verch, Thm.~5.8.)} $\omega$ satisfies the wave front set condition $\mathrm{WF}'(\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}) = C^{(\pm)}$ exactly when its two-point functions have the Hadamard form, in the sense defined there through the squared Dirac operator (the Dirac operator applied to a Hadamard parametrix of its square, plus a smooth kernel). The source poses its CAR results for Majorana spinors; for the Dirac field of four dimensions the class of Hadamard states is treated by Sanders, who fills gaps in the earlier equivalence arguments. The statement of Thm.~5.8 is taken from the source's abstract and introduction, not read against its text.
\item[(b)] \emph{(Propagation; Kratzert, Hollands, Sahlmann and Verch, Sec.~5.2.)} If the two-point functions of $\omega$ have the Hadamard form on an open neighbourhood of one Cauchy surface, they have it on the whole field: Cauchy evolution preserves the Hadamard form of the Dirac field. The argument rests on the propagation of singularities (of polarisation sets) for the Dirac operator, the polarisation set of a Hadamard Dirac two-point function being computed by Kratzert.
\item[(c)] \emph{(Adiabatic states; Hollands.)} On a Robertson-Walker field (spatial sections flat or curved) with smooth scale factor, a homogeneous isotropic gauge-invariant quasi-free state of the massive Dirac field that is adiabatic of infinite order is Hadamard.
\item[(d)] \emph{(Scaling limits; Sahlmann and Verch, Prop.~5.6, Lemma~5.7, Def.~5.3; added in version 2.)} Posed for Majorana spinors on a globally hyperbolic spacetime of dimension $n = 3, 4, 9, 10 \bmod 8$, with Dirac operator $\slashed{\nabla} + im$, $m \ge 0$ (a constant, or a bundle map), and a state Hadamard when near a Cauchy surface its two-point function is $\omega_{2}(f\otimes f') = w(Df\otimes f')$ with $w$ of Hadamard form for the squared operator. Let $\omega$ be a quasi-free Hadamard state, $p$ a point, $\xi_{p}$ normal coordinates at $p$, $\delta_{\lambda}(q) = \xi_{p}(\lambda\,\xi_{p}^{-1}(q))$ the dilations, lifted to the bundle, and $\alpha = \tfrac{n}{2} + \tfrac12$ ($\tfrac52$ in four dimensions) the weight of the dilated test sections. Then, as $\lambda \to 0$, the two-point function of $\omega$ on the dilated test sections converges to $G^{(1)}_{\eta}((\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\Theta R_{*}f)R_{*}f')$, where $G^{(1)}_{\eta}$ is the leading Hadamard distribution of the flat metric in the normal coordinates (with no mass term), $R$ identifies the fibres with $\mathbb{C}^{r}$ through the normal coordinates and a frame, and $\Theta$ is the matrix at $p$ of the Dirac conjugation composed with charge conjugation: the scaling limit of $\omega$ at $p$ is the two-point function of the massless Dirac field on Minkowski space, whatever the mass and the curvature. The limit distributions contain $(p, \xi; p, -\xi)$ in their wave front sets for every $(p, \xi)$ in the set $N^{-}$ of the source (Lemma~5.7).
\end{enumerate}
Not part of this Fact: the converse of (c) (that a homogeneous Hadamard state is adiabatic of infinite order); the transcription of (d) from Majorana to Dirac spinors and from normal-coordinate to other dilations, which the results that use (d) carry out themselves; the source's proof of (d) (its Appendix A.5). \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Kratzert2000}; \cite{Hollands2001}; \cite[Sec.~5.2, Thm.~5.8, Def.~5.3, Prop.~5.6, Lemma~5.7]{SahlmannVerch2001}; for the Dirac equivalence also \cite{Sanders2010}.
synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-p.technical: For the scalar field the store imports that a two-point function of Hadamard form near one instant has that form everywhere. This Fact supplies the same for the Dirac field. For quasi-free states of the free Dirac field on a globally hyperbolic gravitational field, the wave front set form of the Hadamard condition, imposed on both orderings of the two-point function, is equivalent to the Hadamard form defined through the squared Dirac operator (Sahlmann and Verch), and the Hadamard form propagates by Cauchy evolution from a neighbourhood of one Cauchy surface to the whole field; the propagation rests on the propagation of singularities for the Dirac operator, with the polarisation set of a Hadamard Dirac two-point function computed by Kratzert. On Robertson-Walker fields, Hollands showed that the homogeneous Dirac states adiabatic of infinite order, those that agree with the adiabatic expansion of the mode equation to every order in the inverse momentum, are Hadamard. Only that direction is imported; the converse is not. Sahlmann and Verch also determine the short-distance scaling limit of such states: scaled towards a point in normal coordinates, a quasi-free Hadamard state tends to the vacuum two-point function of the massless Dirac field on Minkowski space, whatever the mass and the curvature. Their results for the anticommutation relations are posed for Majorana spinors; Sanders treats the Hadamard states of the four-dimensional Dirac field and fills gaps in the earlier equivalence arguments.
synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-p.lay: Physicists require that a reasonable quantum state of a field, looked at closely enough, resembles empty space. For electrons and the other particles of spin one half, these results show that it is enough to check this at one moment: the equations of motion then keep it true at every other moment. They also show that in a uniformly expanding universe a standard recipe for building states, which follows the expansion smoothly to every order, gives states of this regular kind, and that close up such a state looks exactly like the empty state of massless particles in flat space. These are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extens.formal:
Signature $(+,-,-,-)$, units $\hbar = c = 1$; free fields on flat spacetime, Wick polynomials of them, and a local interaction density $\mathcal{L}$ smeared with a test function $g$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Causal perturbation theory.)} The time-ordered products $T_{n}$ of Wick polynomials are constructed by induction on $n$ from causal factorisation ($T_{n}$ factorises into lower products when the points are causally ordered); at each order $T_{n}$ is fixed by the lower orders away from the total diagonal, and the only freedom is its extension across the diagonal, which can be chosen Poincar\'e covariant; the S-matrix and the interacting fields (Bogoliubov's formula) are formal power series in $g$ built from the $T_{n}$, with no ultraviolet regulator \cite{EpsteinGlaser1973}.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Extension by scaling degree.)} Let $t_{0}$ be a distribution on $\R^{n}\setminus\{0\}$ of scaling degree $\mathrm{sd}$ at the origin. If $\mathrm{sd} < n$ there is a unique extension $t$ to $\R^{n}$ with the same scaling degree. If $n \le \mathrm{sd} < \infty$, extensions with the same scaling degree exist, and two of them differ by $\sum_{|a| \le \omega}c_{a}\partial^{a}\delta$, $\omega = \mathrm{sd} - n$ \cite{BrunettiFredenhagen2000}. The same holds locally on any globally hyperbolic gravitational field, the scaling degree being read in local coordinates.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Ward-preserving time-ordered products in electrodynamics.)} In quantum electrodynamics with the covariant (Gupta-Bleuler) photon the extensions of (i) can be normalised at every order so that perturbative gauge invariance holds; it implies the Ward identities, in particular the Ward-Takahashi identity of the vertex and the self-energy and the transversality of the vacuum polarisation \cite{Scharf1995, Grigore1999}.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Local construction and BRST structure in electrodynamics.)} The interacting fields of (i) generate local algebras without the adiabatic limit; for electrodynamics the BRST transformation is a graded derivation of the interacting field algebra, implemented by a local Kugo-Ojima operator, and the positive Hilbert space structure of the physical states of the free theory is stable under the perturbation \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Yang-Mills.)} Perturbative Yang-Mills theory with ghosts and antifields is renormalisable on every globally hyperbolic gravitational field, flat spacetime included, with Ward identities at the renormalised level that keep the interacting BRST current conserved and the interacting BRST charge nilpotent; the physical observables are the BRST cohomology \cite{Hollands2008}.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extens.technical: Causal perturbation theory, due to Epstein and Glaser, builds the time-ordered products of an interacting quantum field theory order by order from causality alone. At each order the product is already determined away from the points where all arguments coincide; the ultraviolet problem is only how to extend a distribution across that set, and no regulator is introduced. Brunetti and Fredenhagen put the extension step in a local form ordered by the scaling degree: a distribution of scaling degree below the dimension has one extension of the same degree, and at or above the dimension extensions exist and differ by finitely many derivatives of the delta function, the local counterterms. For electrodynamics Scharf showed in this framework that the free normalisation can be chosen so that gauge invariance, and with it the Ward identities, hold at every order (a later proof by Grigore repairs a step that rests on reduction formulae). Duetsch and Fredenhagen constructed the local algebras of interacting fields and implemented the BRST symmetry of electrodynamics by a local Kugo-Ojima operator, with the positivity of the physical states preserved. Hollands extended the construction to Yang-Mills theory on any globally hyperbolic gravitational field, with Ward identities that keep the interacting BRST charge nilpotent.
synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extens.lay: The infinities of quantum field theory can be avoided without any artificial cut-off. Epstein and Glaser showed that the calculation can be built up step by step from the requirement that cause precedes effect; the only freedom left at each step is how to treat the points where particles meet, and that freedom is a short list of constants. Later work showed that this freedom can be used to keep the conservation of electric charge exact at every step, constructed the local quantities of the theory directly, and extended the construction to the force fields of the strong and weak interactions, on flat spacetime and in gravitational fields. The series takes these results from the literature.

synthesis.imported-fewster-lang-spin-pro.formal:
Let a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) have an ultrastatic derived metric on a slab, the product of a time interval $(-T/2, T/2)$ with a compact spatial section $\Sigma$, oriented and globally hyperbolic, and consider the quantised free Dirac field of mass $m$ on it. Weight the spacetime spin product $\int\bar{\psi}\phi$ of two solutions by a nonnegative integrable function $f$ of time; on the space of solutions with the conserved-current inner product it is represented by a bounded self-adjoint operator, and the positive spectral projection of that operator defines a gauge-invariant, pure, quasi-free state, the state extracted from the fermionic projector of Finster and Reintjes \cite{FinsterReintjes2015}, the Dirac analogue of the Sorkin-Johnston state of a scalar field \cite{FewsterLang2015}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For the sharp weight, $f$ the indicator function of the slab, the state fails to be Hadamard for generic lifetimes $T$ (\cite{FewsterLang2015}, Thm.~3.4).
\item[(ii)] For $f$ smooth, compactly supported in the slab, nonnegative and not identically zero, the resulting softened state is Hadamard (\cite{FewsterLang2015}, Thm.~3.5).
\item[(iii)] The Hadamard condition of these states is tied to the finiteness of the fluctuations of Wick polynomials \cite{FewsterLang2015}.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Beyond one flat chart:} the compactness of the spatial section $\Sigma$ is a global ingredient of the setting of the theorems.
synthesis.imported-fewster-lang-spin-pro.technical: On a short stretch of time, a slab, one can build a state of the Dirac field from the field alone: weight the spin product of two solutions over spacetime, compare it with the conserved charge product, and keep the positive part. Fewster and Lang showed that this state, the finite-time form of Finster and Reintjes's fermionic projector and the Dirac analogue of the Sorkin-Johnston state, is pure and quasi-free, but on an ultrastatic slab with compact spatial sections it is generically not Hadamard if the weight is sharp in time; softened with a smooth weight that vanishes near the ends of the slab, it is Hadamard.
synthesis.imported-fewster-lang-spin-pro.lay: A natural way to pick out a quantum state of the electron field, using only the field's own structure over a finite stretch of time, gives a state that is too rough at short distances when the stretch has sharp ends. Fewster and Lang proved this, and showed that smoothing the ends repairs it. The series uses their result when testing whether that construction could select the state left behind by the descent.

synthesis.imported-free-field-spin-stati.technical: The free massless field's vacuum correlation is $-1/(4\pi^{2})$ over the spacetime interval with a small imaginary shift fixing the analytic continuation; at spacelike separation it is real and even. Pauli used this to show that a free field of integer spin must commute and one of half-integer spin must anticommute at spacelike separation if the state space has positive norm, the free-field form of the spin-statistics connection. Guido and Longo proved an algebraic version for interacting fields: if the vacuum's modular flow on each wedge is the wedge's boost (modular covariance), and the net has the Reeh-Schlieder property and normal commutation relations, then the operator grading Bose and Fermi fields is the rotation by $2\pi$; positive energy follows and need not be assumed.
synthesis.imported-free-field-spin-stati.lay: Particles of whole-number spin behave as bosons and those of half-number spin as fermions. For free particles this follows from a short argument of Pauli using the standard formula for how a field's values at two points are correlated. For interacting fields Guido and Longo proved it from a property of the vacuum: that its natural flow in each wedge of spacetime is the geometric boost. The series takes these results as given.

synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-o.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric $g$ is smooth and globally hyperbolic on a region $U$ of its invertible region, $N \subset U$ geodesically convex, $\sigma$ the Synge function of $g$ on $N\times N$ ($\sigma = \tfrac12 Q(x - x')$ on the flat field) and $\Delta$ its Van Vleck determinant.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Bundle parametrix; Friedlander; B\"ar, Ginoux and Pf\"affle, Ch.~2.)} A normally hyperbolic operator $P$ on a vector bundle over $N$ (principal part that of the d'Alembertian of $g$) is, uniquely, the d'Alembertian of a connection $\nabla^{P}$ plus a zero-order term. Its Hadamard coefficients are the unique sections fixed by transport equations along the geodesics from $x'$ with the identity at coincidence, and the leading one is $\Delta^{1/2}(x, x')\,\Pi(x, x')$, $\Pi(x, x')$ the parallel transport of $\nabla^{P}$ along the geodesic from $x'$ to $x$. In four dimensions the Hadamard parametrix of $P$ is, up to its normalising constant, $U/\sigma + V\log\sigma + W$ with $U = \Delta^{1/2}\Pi$ and $V$, $W$ smooth.
\item[(b)] \emph{(The squared Dirac operator; Lichnerowicz.)} Let $\psi$ be the free Dirac field of mass $m \ge 0$ on $(\hb, \Omega)$, with covariant derivative $D_{a}\psi = a\cdot\nabla\psi + \tfrac12\Omega(a)\psi$ and Dirac operator $D = g^{\mu}D_{e_{\mu}}$, $g^{\mu} = \hb^{T}(e^{\mu})$; on massive lines the field theory's unit stands outside the Clifford product, as the right unit $R_{I_{4}}: \psi \mapsto \psi I_{4}$. The squared operator $(R_{I_{4}}D - m)(R_{I_{4}}D + m) = -(D^{2} + m^{2})$ is normally hyperbolic, and by the Lichnerowicz formula ($D^{2}$ is the d'Alembertian of the spin connection plus a multiple of the scalar curvature) its connection $\nabla^{P}$ is the spin connection. So $\Pi(x, x')$ is left multiplication by the rotor $R$ of the geodesic $\gamma$ from $x'$ ($t = 0$) to $x$ ($t = 1$), $\dot R = -\tfrac12\Omega(\dot\gamma)R$, $R = 1$ at $t = 0$ (parallel transport, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(ii)), and the leading Hadamard coefficient of the squared Dirac operator is $U = \Delta^{1/2}R$.
\item[(c)] \emph{(The $i0$ prescription; Kay and Wald; Sahlmann and Verch, Sec.~5.1.)} The distributions $1/\sigma$ and $\log\sigma$ of the Hadamard form are the $\epsilon \to 0^{+}$ limits of their regularisations by $\epsilon(t(x) - t(x'))$ and $\epsilon^{2}$, for a time function $t$ (a smooth function with future-directed timelike unit gradient), as in the source; the Hadamard form so defined, for the scalar field and for vector-valued fields such as the Dirac field, does not depend on the choice of time function. This concerns the bulk distributions on $N\times N$.
\item[(d)] \emph{(Fundamental solutions in four dimensions; Friedlander; B\"ar, Ginoux and Pf\"affle, Ch.~2; for scalar and vector fields Poisson, Secs.~4.3.2, 4.4.2.)} On a geodesically convex, causally convex domain $N$ (a causal domain), with $\sigma$ positive on timelike separation, a time function $t$, and $P$ normalised so that its principal part is $g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}$ (on the flat field the d'Alembertian $\partial_{t}^{2} - \nabla^{2}$), the retarded and advanced fundamental solutions of $P$ ($PG_{\pm} = \delta$, $G_{\pm}(\cdot, x')$ supported in $J^{\pm}(x')$) are
\[
G_{\pm}(x, x') = \frac{1}{4\pi}\,\theta\bigl(\pm(t(x) - t(x'))\bigr)\bigl[U(x, x')\,\delta(\sigma) + V(x, x')\,\theta(\sigma)\bigr],
\]
with $U = \Delta^{1/2}\Pi$ the leading coefficient of (a) and $V$ smooth on $N\times N$; on the flat field $\tfrac{1}{4\pi}\theta(t)\delta(\sigma) = \theta(t)\delta(t - r)/(4\pi r)$. For the squared Dirac operator $D^{2} + m^{2}$ of (b), $U = \Delta^{1/2}R$.
\end{enumerate}
Not part of this Fact: the higher Hadamard coefficients, the covariant expansion of $\Delta$, the coefficient of the curvature term in the Lichnerowicz formula, the normalising constant of the parametrix, and restrictions of the regularised distributions of (c) to null hypersurfaces, which depend on the time function by smooth kernels. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Friedlander1975}; \cite[Ch.~2]{BarGinouxPfaffle2007}; \cite[Secs.~3.5, 5.1]{SahlmannVerch2001}; \cite{KayWald1991}; \cite{Radzikowski1996}; for the transport equations \cite[Def./Prop.~2.10]{Ronge2026}; for the spinor coefficient in two dimensions \cite[Eq.~(52)]{Lewis2020}; for (d) in the scalar and vector cases \cite[Secs.~4.3.2, 4.4.2]{Poisson2004}.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-o.technical: The Hadamard condition says that at short distances the two-point function of a state looks like the vacuum's, and it is written with an explicit singular term built from the squared geodesic distance $\sigma$ between the two points. For a field with several components, the coefficient of the leading singular term is a matrix: the square root of the Van Vleck determinant, which measures how geodesics from a point spread, times the parallel transport of the field's connection along the geodesic joining the two points. For the Dirac field the relevant operator is the square of the Dirac operator, whose connection is the spin connection, so in Gauge Theory Gravity the transport is left multiplication by the rotor that solves $\dot R = -\tfrac12\Omega(\dot\gamma)R$ along the geodesic. The singular terms carry an infinitesimal imaginary shift fixed by a time function, and the resulting Hadamard form is the same for every time function. In four dimensions the retarded and advanced solutions of the squared operator have the same coefficient: a delta function on the light cone with that coefficient, plus a smooth tail inside the cone. These are standard results taken from the literature.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-o.lay: Physicists describe the regular states of a quantum field by the exact way its correlations blow up when two points come together. For the electron field, the strength of that blow-up is set by two pieces of geometry: how quickly straight paths from a point spread out, and how the electron's spin is carried along the path joining the two points. The rule also does not depend on which way of slicing space-time into moments is used to state it, and the same two pieces of geometry fix how a disturbance of the field spreads along the light cone. These are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-hadamard-stress-tenso.formal: Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is the Reissner-Nordstr\"om-de Sitter metric of a charged hole with positive cosmological constant, and let $\phi$ be a free real scalar field on it. For every state of $\phi$ that is Hadamard (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(a)) in the domain of dependence of an initial Cauchy surface, the expected renormalised stress tensor along a radial null geodesic crossing the Cauchy horizon of the hole's interior satisfies $\langle T_{VV}\rangle \sim C/V^{2}$ as $V \to 0$, where $V$ is an affine parameter vanishing at the Cauchy horizon and $C$ is independent of the state and generically nonzero. This divergence is stronger than that of the classical field. \emph{Beyond one flat chart:} the statement concerns the maximal extension of the field through the hole's interior to its Cauchy horizon, read on several charts. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{HollandsWaldZahn2020}.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-stress-tenso.technical: A charged black hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant has, inside, a Cauchy horizon beyond which the future is no longer fixed by the initial data. Classically, perturbations may stay mild there. Hollands, Wald and Zahn showed that a quantum scalar field in any regular (Hadamard) state behaves worse: its expected energy density, measured along a light ray falling through the Cauchy horizon, diverges as the inverse square of the affine distance to it, with a coefficient that does not depend on the state and is generically nonzero. They argue that this makes the Cauchy horizon a strong curvature singularity. For a state set on a collar of an earlier surface, the propagation of the Hadamard form reaches only the domain of dependence of that collar, and at such a Cauchy horizon its stress tensor diverges.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-stress-tenso.lay: Inside a charged black hole there is a boundary beyond which the laws of physics no longer predict what happens from the past. Hollands, Wald and Zahn showed that the energy of a quantum field becomes infinite as one approaches that boundary, whatever regular state the field starts in, which suggests the boundary is destroyed and replaced by a singularity. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: S. Hollands, R. M. Wald and J. Zahn, Quantum instability of the Cauchy horizon in Reissner-Nordstrom-deSitter spacetime, Class. Quantum Grav. 37 (2020), 115009; arXiv:1912.06047.

synthesis.imported-haefner-nicolas-dirac.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric $g$ is smooth on a region $U$ of its invertible region, $p_{0} \in U$, and $\mathcal{O} \subset U$ a geodesically convex, globally hyperbolic neighbourhood of $p_{0}$ with a time function $t$, $t(p_{0}) = 0$, and slices $\Sigma_{T} = \{t = T\}$. Let $\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}$ be the future light cone of $p_{0}$, with its vertex blown up, and $D_{T} = J^{+}(p_{0})\cap\{0 \le t \le T\}$ for $T > 0$ small enough. Consider the Dirac field of mass $m \ge 0$ on $\mathcal{O}$ (an electromagnetic potential is allowed in the source). Then (H\"afner and Nicolas):
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Flux identity; Eq.~(14).)} For a smooth solution $\Psi$ with data on $\Sigma_{T}$, the flux of the conserved Dirac current through $\Sigma_{T}$ equals its flux through $\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}\cap D_{T}$: $\int_{\Sigma_{T}}|\Psi|^{2}\,d\sigma_{\Sigma_{T}} = \int_{\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}}(|\Psi_{1}|^{2} + |\Psi_{4}|^{2})\,d\sigma_{\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}}$, where $\Psi_{1}$, $\Psi_{4}$ are the components of $\Psi$ on the cone, in a spin frame adapted to it, that the flux through the cone sees.
\item[(b)] \emph{(Theorem 1, with the abstract.)} The trace operator $\Gamma$, which takes data on $\Sigma_{T}$ to the pair $(\Psi_{1}, \Psi_{4})$ on the cone, extends to an isometry from $L^{2}$ data on $\Sigma_{T}$ to $L^{2}(\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}, d\sigma)\otimes\mathbb{C}^{2}$; the characteristic Cauchy problem on the cone has, for $L^{2}$ data, a unique solution in the future of the cone within $D_{T}$, so $\Gamma$ is unitary.
\item[(c)] \emph{(Theorem 2.)} $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism from $H^{1}(\Sigma_{T})$ onto the space of cone data whose $(\Psi_{1}, \Psi_{4})$ and their derivatives along the null tetrad are square integrable.
\end{enumerate}
Not part of this Fact: null hypersurfaces other than light cones near their vertex, the part of the cone beyond $t = T$, and any statement about states. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{HafnerNicolas2011}, Def.~3.6, Def.~4.2, Eq.~(14), Theorems 1 and 2.
synthesis.imported-haefner-nicolas-dirac.technical: On a null hypersurface the Dirac field is determined by only half of its components, the ones that the flow of the conserved current through the hypersurface sees. Häfner and Nicolas proved, for the light cone of a point in an arbitrary spacetime, close enough to the vertex, that these two components on the cone carry exactly the same norm as the full field on a spacelike slice (the current is conserved, so what flows through the slice flows through the cone), and that every square-integrable choice of them comes from exactly one solution. The trace on the cone is therefore unitary, which is the statement that the field restricted to the light rays of the cone obeys the canonical anticommutation relations. They also identify the cone data that give solutions with one square-integrable derivative. The field may be massive. This is a standard result taken from the literature, for light cones near the vertex only.
synthesis.imported-haefner-nicolas-dirac.lay: Along a sheet of light rays the electron field is fixed by only half of its parts. For the light cone of a point, close to its tip, in any gravitational field, mathematicians proved that those parts carry exactly the same information as the whole field at an instant, with nothing lost and nothing extra. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: D. Häfner and J.-P. Nicolas, The characteristic Cauchy problem for Dirac fields on curved backgrounds, J. Hyperbolic Differ. Equ. 8 (2011), no. 3, 437--483; arXiv:0903.0515.

synthesis.imported-heat-kernel-coefficie.technical: The heat kernel of a second-order operator of Laplace type has a small-time expansion whose coefficients are integrals of local invariants: the endomorphism part $E$, the curvature $\Omega$ of the connection and the curvature of the manifold. Vassilevich labels them by the power $t^{(k-n)/2}$, so the coefficient that carries $E^{2}$ and $\Omega^{2}$ is his $a_{4}$; DeWitt labels by integer powers and calls it $a_{2}$. On a flat background its field-strength part is $\tfrac12E^{2} + \tfrac1{12}\Omega^{2}$, and it multiplies the logarithm of the cut-off in the one-loop determinant. In the background-field gauge of Abbott the gauge fixing respects the gauge symmetry of the background, so the one-loop effective action is a gauge-invariant function of the background field strength, and the coefficient of its square gives the running of the coupling; each field contributes the determinant of its one-loop operator, weighted by its statistics and by whether it is real or complex, with the Faddeev-Popov ghosts entering as a complex scalar with fermionic sign.
synthesis.imported-heat-kernel-coefficie.lay: How strongly the forces of nature act changes with the energy at which they are probed, and the rate of change at the first quantum level can be read from a standard expansion that describes how heat would spread on the space of field configurations. Combined with a standard way of fixing the redundancy of force fields that keeps their symmetry visible, the expansion gives each kind of particle's contribution to the running. These are textbook results that the series takes as given.

synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-s.technical: Kuckert's theorem derives the spin-statistics connection of a theory of local observables from a weak modular assumption: the modular conjugation of each wedge, defined by the vacuum, acts on the local algebras as the wedge's spacetime reflection. With covariance under the covering group, the spectrum condition and a compact internal symmetry group, the rotation by $2\pi$ is then a product of modular conjugations of wedges turned by half that angle, trivial on observables, and on the Doplicher-Roberts field algebra it is the Bose-Fermi grading. The modular groups themselves need not act as boosts, so the assumption is weaker than full modular covariance. Borchers's theorem supplies the relation between the modular objects of an algebra and a positive-energy translation that maps the algebra into itself: the modular group dilates the translations at rate $2\pi$, and the modular conjugation reverses them.
synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-s.lay: Why particles of half-integer spin obey the exclusion rule can be proved in several ways. Kuckert showed that it follows from a symmetry property of the vacuum: the mathematical reflection that the vacuum defines for each wedge-shaped region of spacetime must act on what can be measured as the ordinary mirror reflection of that wedge. Borchers's theorem, a tool of the same theory, says how this reflection and its companion flow treat a shift along a light ray that carries the region into itself. The series uses both when asking which assumption would carry its spin and statistics results beyond approximations.

synthesis.imported-lsz-reduction-ward-id.technical: Three standard results of quantum electrodynamics. The reduction formula of Lehmann, Symanzik and Zimmermann turns time-ordered correlation functions into scattering amplitudes: each external particle contributes a pole at its mass shell, the amplitude is the residue, and each leg carries the square root of the field's normalisation constant. Ward's identity ties the electron-photon vertex at zero momentum transfer to the momentum derivative of the electron self-energy, so the vertex and electron-field renormalisation constants are equal and only the photon field renormalises the charge. Jost and Luttinger computed the vacuum polarisation to fourth order in the charge, the second coefficient of the running of the fine-structure constant: per Dirac fermion $\mu\,d\alpha/d\mu = 2\alpha^{2}/(3\pi) + \alpha^{3}/(2\pi^{2})$.
synthesis.imported-lsz-reduction-ward-id.lay: Three classic results of the quantum theory of light and electrons: the rule that turns the theory's correlation functions into probabilities for particles to scatter; Ward's identity, which guarantees that the electron's charge is corrected only through the light field and never separately through the electron; and the second-order calculation of how the strength of the electric force grows with energy. The series takes these from the literature.

synthesis.imported-luscher-mack-conforma.formal: Let a quantum field theory on Minkowski space (the flat gravitational field, $\hb = 1$, $\Omega = 0$; Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) satisfy the Wightman axioms and be conformally invariant, in the sense that its Euclidean Green functions are invariant under the Euclidean conformal group. Then (L\"uscher and Mack) the theory extends to the universal covering $\widetilde{M}$ of compactified Minkowski space, on which the universal covering of the conformal group $\mathrm{SO}(2,4)$ acts by a unitary representation on the state space; $\widetilde{M}$ carries the derived metric of the Einstein static field $\mathbb{R} \times S^{3}$ of unit radius, conformal to Minkowski space on the image of the embedding. The conformal energy $H = \tfrac12(P_{0} + K_{0})$, the combination of the time translation $P_{0}$ and the special conformal generator $K_{0}$ of Minkowski space, generates the time translations of $\mathbb{R} \times S^{3}$: it is the energy of the theory on the unit Einstein static field, and its spectrum is bounded below. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{LuscherMack1975}. \emph{Beyond one flat chart.} $\widetilde{M}$ and the Einstein static field are global and are read on several charts of flat spacetime, each with its own gravitational field, glued by gauge transformations; the conformal embedding of Minkowski space into one of them is stated on one chart.
synthesis.imported-luscher-mack-conforma.technical: A conformally invariant field theory on Minkowski space does not live only on Minkowski space: its natural home is the universal covering of the conformal compactification, which is the Einstein static universe, a cylinder $\mathbb{R} \times S^{3}$. L\"uscher and Mack showed that, given Euclidean conformal invariance, the Minkowski theory extends there, with the whole covering group of the conformal group acting unitarily. Under this embedding the time translation of the cylinder of unit radius is the conformal Hamiltonian $\tfrac12(P_{0} + K_{0})$ of Minkowski space, so the conformal energy of a state on Minkowski space is its energy on the unit Einstein static field.
synthesis.imported-luscher-mack-conforma.lay: Theories that look the same at every scale can be moved, without losing information, from ordinary flat spacetime onto a closed universe shaped like a cylinder whose cross-section is a three-dimensional sphere. L\"uscher and Mack showed how. On that cylinder an ordinary energy is defined, and it corresponds to a particular combination of energy and a rescaling-type symmetry in flat spacetime. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: M. L\"uscher and G. Mack, Global conformal invariance in quantum field theory, Commun. Math. Phys. 41 (1975), 203--234.

synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-an.formal:
Signature $(+,-,-,-)$, $\ell^{2} = Q(\ell)$, units $\hbar = c = 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Feynman parametrisation.)} For nonzero $D_{1}, \ldots, D_{n}$ of one sign, $\dfrac{1}{D_{1}\cdots D_{n}} = (n-1)!\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\!dx_{1}\cdots dx_{n}\,\frac{\delta(1 - \sum_{j}x_{j})}{(\sum_{j}x_{j}D_{j})^{n}}$ \cite{Weinzierl2010}.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Wick-rotated integrals.)} After the rotation $\ell_{0} = i\ell_{E,0}$, which takes $\int d^{4}\ell\,f(-\ell^{2})$ to $i\int d^{4}\ell_{E}\,f(\ell_{E}^{2})$ \cite{Weinzierl2010}, for $\Delta > 0$: $\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}(\ell^{2} - \Delta)^{-3} = \frac{-i}{32\pi^{2}\Delta}$; with the Euclidean cut-off $\ell_{E}^{2} \le L$, $\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}(\ell^{2} - \Delta)^{-2} = \frac{i}{16\pi^{2}}\bigl(\ln(L/\Delta) - 1 + O(\Delta/L)\bigr)$. Terms odd in $\ell$ integrate to zero and $\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta} \to \tfrac14 Q(\ell)g^{\alpha\beta}$ under the integral (symmetric integration) \cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Pauli-Villars regulators.)} Each internal line of mass $m$ is replaced by a weighted sum over fields of masses $M_{i}$ and weights $c_{i}$, $c_{0} = 1$, $M_{0} = m$, with $\sum_{i}c_{i} = \sum_{i}c_{i}M_{i}^{2} = 0$; the weights take both signs, and a field of negative weight is quantised with a negative metric. At one loop these conditions make the integrals of (ii) finite, the regularisation is Lorentz invariant and keeps the Ward identity of electrodynamics, and the physical limit is $M_{i} \to \infty$ for $i \ge 1$ \cite{PauliVillars1949}. A regulator of a single Weyl fermion is a Dirac field of mass $M_{i}$, so the scheme does not preserve chirality.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Covariant photon.)} In the covariant (Gupta-Bleuler) quantisation the photon propagator in the gauge with parameter $\xi$ is $\frac{-i}{k^{2} + i0}\bigl(g_{\mu\nu} - (1 - \xi)\frac{k_{\mu}k_{\nu}}{k^{2}}\bigr)$, $\xi = 1$ the Feynman gauge, and on-shell amplitudes between physical external states are independent of $\xi$ by the Ward identity \cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}.
\item[(v)] \emph{(On-shell external states.)} Scattering amplitudes are evaluated between on-shell spinors, $(p - m)u(p) = 0$, so between external states a Dirac line carries the projector $(p + m)/(2m)$ (LSZ reduction) \cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-an.technical: These are the standard tools for computing one-loop corrections in a relativistic quantum field theory. Feynman's trick combines a product of propagator denominators into one power of a weighted sum over the simplex. The loop momentum is then shifted, the integral rotated to Euclidean signature, and terms odd in the momentum dropped while products of two momenta are replaced by a quarter of the square times the metric; the remaining integrals are elementary, finite for three denominators and logarithmically divergent for two. Pauli and Villars regulate by adding heavy copies of each field with weights of both signs, chosen so that the weights and the weighted squared masses sum to zero: this is relativistically invariant and respects the conservation of charge, but the copies of negative weight are fields of negative norm, and a regulated chiral fermion acquires a mass. In covariant quantisation the photon propagator carries a gauge parameter on which physical on-shell amplitudes do not depend, and external lines are on-shell spinors.
synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-an.lay: To compute the first quantum corrections in a theory such as electrodynamics, physicists use a standard toolkit: a trick for combining denominators, a rotation of the time direction into an imaginary one that turns the integrals into ordinary ones, and a way of taming their infinities with heavy auxiliary particles, some of which count negatively. These tools are textbook material; the series takes them as given.

imported_from.citation: W. Pauli and F. Villars, On the invariant regularization in relativistic quantum theory, Rev. Mod. Phys. 21 (1949), 434--444.
M. E. Peskin and D. V. Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory, Addison-Wesley (1995), chapters 6 and 7.
S. Weinzierl, Introduction to Feynman integrals, arXiv:1005.1855, equations (50) and (61).

synthesis.imported-quasi-spin-pairing-an.technical: Kerman's quasi-spin method solves the pairing model of nuclear physics exactly if all the levels are degenerate: the pair creation and annihilation operators form an $\su(2)$, so the energies follow from the Casimir and depend only on the particle number and the seniority, the number of unpaired particles. Breaking one pair costs the pairing strength times the pair degeneracy. Nambu and Jona-Lasinio found the particle-physics analogue: a fermion that gets its mass dynamically has a scalar partner at twice its mass. Assuming the top quark is the sole constituent, this gives the classic top-condensation prediction of a Higgs at twice the top mass, which more elaborate models with several condensates bring down to the observed value.
synthesis.imported-quasi-spin-pairing-an.lay: When particles pair up, as electrons do in a superconductor and nucleons in a nucleus, it costs a definite energy to break a pair, and for the simplest model this is known exactly. Particle physicists borrowed the idea: if the Higgs boson were a bound pair of top quarks, the simplest estimate puts it at twice the top's mass, far heavier than observed, though models with several kinds of pairs can bring it down. The series takes these results as given.

synthesis.imported-renormalised-stress-t.formal: Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is smooth and globally hyperbolic, and let $\psi$ be the free Dirac field on it, formulated as a locally covariant quantum field theory. Wick polynomials of $\psi$ are defined by point splitting with the Hadamard parametrix subtracted (the extended algebra of observables). On every Hadamard state $\omega$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(b)) they give an expected stress-energy tensor $\langle T_{ab}\rangle_{\omega}$, a smooth symmetric tensor field of the derived metric, which is covariantly conserved, $\nabla^{a}\langle T_{ab}\rangle_{\omega} = 0$; its trace anomaly is computed explicitly there. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{DappiaggiHackPinamonti2009}. Cited from memory, not part of the checked statement: that the trace anomaly is a local polynomial in the curvature and the mass, the same for every state; that the renormalised tensor is fixed up to local covariant terms built from the curvature and the mass; and that the difference of the tensors of two Hadamard states, the coincidence limit of a differential operator applied to their smooth difference kernel, needs no renormalisation.
synthesis.imported-renormalised-stress-t.technical: A quantum field's energy density cannot be read off its two-point function directly, since the coincidence limit is infinite; on Hadamard states the infinite part is the same universal singularity for every state and can be subtracted geometrically. Dappiaggi, Hack and Pinamonti carried this out for the Dirac field on any globally hyperbolic gravitational field, in the locally covariant framework: they defined Wick polynomials of the spinor field by subtracting the Hadamard parametrix, and with them a stress-energy tensor that is covariantly conserved on Hadamard states and so can act as the source of the gravitational field equations. Its trace is the trace anomaly, which they computed. The tensor is defined only on Hadamard states, and the remaining freedom is in local curvature terms common to all states.
synthesis.imported-renormalised-stress-t.lay: In a gravitational field the energy carried by a quantum field can be computed only for well-behaved quantum states, called Hadamard states, by removing an infinite part that is the same for all of them. For electrons and the other particles of spin one half this was worked out by Dappiaggi, Hack and Pinamonti, who showed that the resulting energy and momentum are conserved, so they can serve as the source in the equations of gravity. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: C. Dappiaggi, T.-P. Hack and N. Pinamonti, The extended algebra of observables for Dirac fields and the trace anomaly of their stress-energy tensor, Rev. Math. Phys. 21 (2009), 1241--1312; arXiv:0904.0612.

synthesis.imported-schwinger-term-and-ma.technical: For fermions in one chiral band with the negative levels filled, the Fourier modes of the density do not commute: the commutator of a mode with its conjugate equals the momentum, a central term. It makes the density modes a set of boson modes, the basis of bosonisation (Tomonaga; Mattis and Lieb, who noticed the care the normal ordering needs). For any finite band the term is absent; it comes from the infinite sea. In relativistic field theory the same structure appears as Schwinger's term in the commutator of charge and current densities, which a positive-energy vacuum forces to be nonzero.
synthesis.imported-schwinger-term-and-ma.lay: In a one-dimensional sea of fermions, ripples of density behave exactly like independent bosons, a standard result of the 1950s and 1960s. The reason is a small extra term in how density ripples combine, which comes from the infinitely deep sea of filled levels; Schwinger showed the same kind of term must appear in any relativistic theory with a stable vacuum. The series takes these results as given.

synthesis.imported-singer-gauge-slice-ne.technical: These are the standard non-perturbative limits of gauge fixing and the standard phase structure of lattice gauge theories with Higgs fields. Singer showed that Gribov's observation is topological: on the three- or four-sphere no continuous condition picks one representative from every gauge orbit of a non-abelian field. Neuberger showed that a BRST gauge fixing on the lattice fails globally: summing over the Gribov copies with the signs of their Faddeev-Popov determinants gives the Euler characteristic of the compact gauge group, zero, so the partition function and every expectation value become $0/0$. Fradkin and Shenker showed that with a Higgs field in the fundamental representation the Higgs and confining regimes of a lattice gauge theory are one phase: no sharp order parameter separates them.
synthesis.imported-singer-gauge-slice-ne.lay: Describing the force fields of particle physics involves a redundancy, and the usual ways of removing it work only for weak fields. Singer proved that no smooth way of removing it works everywhere; Neuberger showed that the standard bookkeeping, done on a lattice of spacetime points, gives zero divided by zero; and Fradkin and Shenker showed that a force field with a Higgs field of the simplest kind has no sharp boundary between a regime where its charges are confined and one where its particles are massive. The series takes these results from the literature.

synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-.technical: Wilson put gauge theory on a spacetime lattice with group-valued link variables and the action built from the trace of the product around each elementary square; the theory is gauge invariant with no gauge fixing, its coupling is $\beta = 2N/g^{2}$ for $SU(N)$, and it reduces to Yang-Mills theory as the lattice spacing shrinks. Under strong coupling Wilson loops fall with the area they enclose, which is confinement of static charges. Osterwalder and Seiler proved that these lattice theories have a positive transfer matrix, so they describe quantum theories at finite spacing, and proved the strong-coupling area law rigorously. Elitzur showed that a local symmetry cannot break spontaneously on the lattice. The strong-coupling area law does not distinguish abelian from non-abelian groups: four-dimensional compact $U(1)$ also confines at strong coupling, but it is proved to have a deconfined, massless phase at weak coupling.
synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-.lay: Putting the forces of nature on a grid of points in space and time, as Wilson did in 1974, avoids the redundancy problems of their usual description and makes it possible to prove things about them. On such a grid, if the coupling is strong, a pair of test charges is held together with a force that does not weaken with distance. This is proved rigorously, but it holds for electromagnetism on a grid too, which is known to stop confining at weak coupling, so it is not by itself evidence that the real strong force confines.
